H1.text: A leaf pressed flat inside an old book. A frog kept in a glass jar. A tree with a name board in a garden.

H2.text: Three odd things. But all three help scientists name living things correctly.

H3.text: Diya found a dried leaf between the pages of her grandfather's old book. She asked: why would anyone keep a dead leaf for years?

H4.text: Scientists keep huge collections like this on purpose. Today you meet these tools, the taxonomic aids, and learn to use a key yourself.

B1.text: So what is a taxonomic aid?

B2.text: To classify a living thing, you first have to identify it. You compare it with things that are already named.

B3.text: Taxonomic aids are the collections and records that make this comparison possible.

B4.text: There are five you must know. The herbarium, the botanical garden, the museum, the zoological park, and the key.

Z1.text: Let's start with the herbarium, and build one sheet.

Z2.text: A herbarium is a store house of plant specimens. Each one is dried, pressed, and kept on a sheet.

Z3.text: Here is one sheet. The pressed plant is fixed on stiff paper, with its leaves, stem, and a flower.

Z4.text: In the corner sits the label. It carries the date and the place of collection, and the plant's English, local and botanical names.

Z5.text: It also gives the family, and the name of the person who collected it.

Z6.text: Then the sheets are stored in cupboards, arranged in a system of classification that scientists everywhere accept.

P1.text: Now watch how one sheet is made, stage by stage.

P2.text: Collect. A healthy plant part is picked, with leaves and flowers if possible.

P3.text: Press. It is laid flat between sheets of paper and squeezed.

P4.text: Dry. The paper soaks up the water, until the plant is fully dry.

P5.text: Mount. The dry plant is fixed on a herbarium sheet.

P6.text: Label and store. The label is filled in, and the sheet joins the collection.

G1.text: Next, three more places that hold real specimens.

G2.text: A botanical garden grows living plants for reference. Each plant carries a label with its botanical name and its family.

G3.text: Famous ones are the Royal Botanical Garden at Kew in England, the Indian Botanical Garden at Howrah, and the National Botanical Research Institute in Lucknow.

G4.text: A museum keeps preserved specimens. Some sit in jars of preserving liquid. Insects are pinned in insect boxes. Birds and mammals are stuffed, and skeletons are kept too.

G5.text: A zoological park keeps wild animals in a protected place, close to their natural home. Here we learn their food habits and behaviour.

C1.text: Two of these are easy to mix up.

C2.text: A herbarium holds dead plants: dried, pressed, and kept on sheets.

C3.text: A botanical garden holds living plants, growing in the ground, each with its label.

C4.text: Your turn. A teacher wants students to watch one tree flower and fruit over a whole year. Herbarium, or botanical garden? Pause and decide.

C5.text: Botanical garden! Only a living plant can flower and fruit. A herbarium sheet never changes.

K1.text: Now the fifth aid, and the one you can use with a pencil. The key.

K2.text: A key helps you identify an organism by answering pairs of choices.

K3.text: Each pair shows two opposite features. This pair is called a couplet.

K4.text: Each single statement in the pair is called a lead. You pick one lead, and it sends you to the next couplet, or gives you the name.

T1.text: Remember this. A key always offers two opposite choices at a time.

W1.text: Now, a worked example. Let's run four animals through a key: a crow, a cat, a frog, and a housefly.

W2.text: Couplet one. Backbone present, or no backbone? The housefly has no backbone, so it leaves here.

W3.text: Couplet two. Body covered with feathers, or no feathers? The crow has feathers, so it leaves here.

W4.text: Couplet three. Body covered with hair, or moist skin without hair? The cat has hair. The frog has moist skin.

W5.text: Three couplets, four animals, four names. Every step was one clear choice between two leads.

X2.text: Many students call each statement in a key a couplet.

X3.text: But each single statement is a lead. A couplet is the pair of two opposite leads.

E1.text: Where is this asked? This part is not in the current NCERT text. If it comes up, expect statement questions on the herbarium label, or on couplets and leads.

Q1.text: Exam level now. Match each aid with its feature. Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is D. One r, two p, three s, four q.

A2.text: A herbarium keeps dried, pressed plants on sheets. A botanical garden grows living plants with labels.

A3.text: A museum pins insects in boxes. And a key is built from couplets of opposite characters.
